name: Show how a single formal neuron with the unit step activation (\(\sigma(\xi)=1\) for \(\xi\ge0\), else 0) computes AND, OR and NOT. Give the weights and justify them.
answer:
All neurons have the formal input \(x_0=1\) with bias \(w_0\) and inner potential \(\xi=w_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_ix_i\); inputs are from \(\{0,1\}\).

\(\mathrm{AND}(x_1,\dots,x_n)\): bias \(w_0=-n\), all weights \(w_i=1\). Then \(\xi=-n+\sum_i x_i\), which is \(\ge0\) iff all \(n\) inputs are 1.

\(\mathrm{OR}(x_1,\dots,x_n)\): bias \(w_0=-1\), all weights \(w_i=1\). Then \(\xi=-1+\sum_i x_i\ge0\) iff at least one input is 1.

\(\mathrm{NOT}(x_1)\): bias \(w_0=0\), weight \(w_1=-1\). Then \(\xi=-x_1\), which is \(\ge0\) (output 1) iff \(x_1=0\), and negative (output 0) for \(x_1=1\).

Geometrically each of these neurons is a hyperplane cutting off the appropriate corner(s) of the Boolean cube \(\{0,1\}^n\).
keyPoints: AND: bias \(-n\), weights 1 → \(\xi=-n+\sum x_i\ge0\) iff all inputs are 1
OR: bias \(-1\), weights 1 → \(\xi\ge0\) iff some input is 1
NOT: bias 0, weight \(-1\) → \(\xi=-x_1\ge0\) iff \(x_1=0\)
Unit step outputs 1 exactly when \(\xi\ge0\)

name: State and prove the theorem about two-layer MLPs (one hidden layer plus the output layer) and Boolean functions.
answer:
Theorem. Let \(\sigma\) be the unit step function. Two-layer MLPs (i.e. with one hidden layer), where each neuron has \(\sigma\) as the activation function, are able to compute all functions of the form \(F:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\).

Proof.
Step 1 – a neuron recognising one vector. Given \(v=(v_1,\dots,v_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\), consider a neuron \(N_v\) with
• bias \(w_0=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_i\),
• weights \(w_i=1\) if \(v_i=1\) and \(w_i=-1\) if \(v_i=0\).
For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) its inner potential is \[ \xi=-\sum_{i}v_i+\sum_{i:\,v_i=1}x_i-\sum_{i:\,v_i=0}x_i=-\sum_{i:\,v_i=1}(1-x_i)-\sum_{i:\,v_i=0}x_i=-d_H(x,v), \] minus the number of positions where \(x\) and \(v\) differ (Hamming distance). So \(\xi=0\) for \(x=v\), giving output 1, and \(\xi\le-1\lt0\) for \(x\ne v\), giving output 0. Hence \(N_v\) outputs 1 iff the input is \(v\).

Step 2 – combine. The hidden layer consists of all neurons \(N_v\) for the vectors \(v\) with \(F(v)=1\). Connect their outputs to an output neuron implementing OR (bias \(-1\), weights 1).

Correctness. For an input \(x\), only \(N_x\) can fire, and it is present in the hidden layer iff \(F(x)=1\). Hence the OR neuron outputs 1 iff \(F(x)=1\), so the network computes \(F\). If \(F\equiv0\), the hidden layer is empty and the output neuron (bias \(-1\), no inputs) outputs 0 for every input – also correct. \(\square\)

Remark: the construction may need up to \(2^n\) hidden neurons.
keyPoints: Theorem: two-layer unit-step MLPs compute every \(F:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\)
Neuron \(N_v\): bias \(-\sum v_i\), weight 1 where \(v_i=1\) and \(-1\) where \(v_i=0\)
\(\xi=-d_H(x,v)\): 0 for \(x=v\), \(\le-1\) otherwise, so \(N_v\) fires iff \(x=v\)
Hidden layer: one neuron \(N_v\) for every \(v\) with \(F(v)=1\)
Output neuron implements OR of the hidden neurons (empty hidden layer for \(F\equiv0\) gives constant 0)
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slide 43 (OR neuron from slide 42); Hamming-distance form of the verification and the case F=0 derived

name: Explain non-linear separation by networks with two hidden layers (three-layer networks) and unit step activations: what does each layer do geometrically, and how can such networks "approximate" any "reasonable" subset of the input space?
answer:
Consider a three-layer network (two hidden layers plus the output layer) in which each neuron has the unit step activation. The network divides the input space into two subspaces according to the output (0 or 1).

Role of the layers:
• The first hidden layer divides the input space into half-spaces (each neuron = one separating hyperplane).
• The second hidden layer may e.g. make intersections of the half-spaces \(\Rightarrow\) convex sets (a neuron implementing AND).
• The output layer may e.g. make unions of some convex sets (a neuron implementing OR).

Approximating any reasonable set \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^{k}\):
1. Cover \(A\) with hypercubes (squares in 2D, cubes in 3D, …).
2. Each hypercube \(K\) can be separated using a two-layer network \(N_K\): the function computed by \(N_K\) gives 1 for points in \(K\) and 0 for the rest (a hypercube is an intersection of half-spaces: first-layer neurons give its faces, a neuron in the next layer their intersection).
3. Finally, connect the outputs of the nets \(N_K\) satisfying \(K\cap A\ne\emptyset\) using a neuron implementing OR.

The resulting network outputs 1 exactly on the union of the selected hypercubes, which approximates \(A\) the better the finer the cover is.
keyPoints: First layer: half-spaces
Second layer: intersections of half-spaces → convex sets
Third layer: unions of convex sets
Cover A with hypercubes; each hypercube K separated by a two-layer net N_K
OR over the nets \(N_K\) with \(K\cap A\ne\emptyset\)

name: Consider two-layer networks (one hidden layer) with a single input and a single output, hidden ReLU neurons \(\sigma(\xi)=\max(\xi,0)\) and an output neuron with identity activation \(\sigma(\xi)=\xi\). (a) State what such networks can approximate and classify. (b) Show how three ReLU neurons form a "tent" function and how a sum of tents gives a piecewise linear approximation. (c) Explain how the classification claim reduces to the approximation claim.
answer:
(a) Claims.
• Function approximation: for every continuous \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) and every \(\varepsilon\gt0\) there is such a network computing \(F:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) with \(\lvert f(x)-F(x)\rvert\le\varepsilon\) for all \(x\in[0,1]\).
• Classification: for every open \(A\subseteq[0,1]\) there is such a network such that for "most" \(x\in[0,1]\): \(x\in A\) iff the output for \(x\) is \(\gt\tfrac12\).

(b) Idea of approximation (the tent construction is derived here as an interpretation of the slides' figure). The network computes a weighted sum of ReLUs, i.e. a continuous piecewise linear function. A "tent" of height \(h\) on \([a,c]\) with peak at \(b=\tfrac{a+c}{2}\) is \[ T(x)=s\,\max(x-a,0)-2s\,\max(x-b,0)+s\,\max(x-c,0),\qquad s=\frac{h}{b-a}. \] Check: for \(x\le a\) all terms are 0; on \([a,b]\) \(T=s(x-a)\) rises to \(h\) at \(b\); on \([b,c]\) \(T=s(x-a)-2s(x-b)=s(2b-a-x)\) falls to \(0\) at \(x=c\) (as \(2b-a=c\)); for \(x\ge c\) the slopes \(s-2s+s\) cancel, so \(T=0\). Summing tents of suitable heights placed next to each other, the output neuron obtains a piecewise linear function that follows \(f\) within \(\varepsilon\) (a continuous function on \([0,1]\) is uniformly approximable by piecewise linear ones when the pieces are short enough).

(c) Classification from approximation. Take \(g(x)=\min\{1,\operatorname{dist}(x,[0,1]\setminus A)/\delta\}\). It is continuous, \(g=0\) outside \(A\), and \(g\lt1\) only on a part of \(A\) whose measure tends to 0 as \(\delta\to0\). Approximate \(g\) within \(\tfrac14\) by a network: then the output is \(\gt\tfrac34\gt\tfrac12\) where \(g=1\) and \(\lt\tfrac14\lt\tfrac12\) outside \(A\), so only the small part of \(A\) where \(g\lt1\) may be misclassified.
keyPoints: Approximation: any continuous \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) within \(\varepsilon\) on all of \([0,1]\)
Classification: any open \(A\subseteq[0,1]\), output \(\gt1/2\) iff \(x\in A\) for "most" \(x\)
Output is a weighted sum of ReLUs = piecewise linear function
Tent = \(s\max(x-a,0)-2s\max(x-b,0)+s\max(x-c,0)\); a sum of tents approximates \(f\)
Classification via \(g(x)=\min\{1,\operatorname{dist}(x,[0,1]\setminus A)/\delta\}\) approximated within \(1/4\)
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 46–47 (slide 47 is a figure; tent formula and its check derived)

name: State Cybenko's theorem in both versions (non-linear separation and function approximation), explain the terms "sigmoidal", "reasonable" and "most", and mention later generalisations of the theorem.
answer:
A continuous function \(\sigma\) is sigmoidal if \(\sigma(x)\to1\) for \(x\to+\infty\) and \(\sigma(x)\to0\) for \(x\to-\infty\).

Theorem (Cybenko 1989 – informal classification version). Let \(\sigma\) be a continuous sigmoidal function. For every "reasonable" set \(A\subseteq[0,1]^n\) there is a two-layer network (one hidden layer), where each hidden neuron has the activation function \(\sigma\) (output neurons are linear), such that for "most" vectors \(v\in[0,1]^n\) we have: \(v\in A\) iff the network output is \(\gt0\) for the input \(v\).
For the mathematically oriented: "reasonable" means Lebesgue measurable; "most" means that the set of incorrectly classified vectors has Lebesgue measure smaller than a given \(\varepsilon\gt0\).

Theorem (Cybenko 1989 – function approximation). Let \(\sigma\) be a continuous sigmoidal function. For every continuous function \(f:[0,1]^n\to[0,1]\) and every \(\varepsilon\gt0\) there is a function \(F:[0,1]^n\to\mathbb R\) computed by a two-layer network (one hidden layer), where each hidden neuron has the activation function \(\sigma\) (output neurons are linear), such that \(\lvert f(v)-F(v)\rvert\lt\varepsilon\) for every \(v\in[0,1]^n\).

Generalisations: the result was shown independently by Hornik, Stinchcombe & White (1989). The same holds for every continuous activation function that is not a polynomial – including ReLU (Leshno, Lin, Pinkus & Schocken 1993).
keyPoints: Sigmoidal: continuous, tends to 1 at \(+\infty\) and to 0 at \(-\infty\)
Two-layer network (one hidden layer), hidden activation σ, linear output neurons
Classification: \(v\in A\) iff output \(\gt0\) for "most" \(v\) (error set of measure \(\lt\varepsilon\))
"Reasonable" = Lebesgue measurable
Approximation: \(\lvert f(v)-F(v)\rvert\lt\varepsilon\) for every \(v\in[0,1]^n\), \(f\) continuous
Holds for every continuous non-polynomial activation, including ReLU

name: The universal approximation theorems concern two-layer networks (one hidden layer). What is known today "beyond two layers" – about size, depth, width, transformers and the relation between expressivity and learnability?
answer:
• Size: the theorems say nothing about size – the hidden layer may need to be astronomically large.
• Depth helps: there are functions computable by small deep networks that any shallow network can approximate only with exponentially many neurons (Telgarsky 2016; Eldan & Shamir 2016).
• Width is not everything: deep ReLU networks with only \(n+1\) neurons per layer are universal approximators of continuous functions on \([0,1]^n\) (Hanin & Sellke 2017).
• Transformers (later in the course) approximate any continuous sequence-to-sequence function.
• Expressivity \(\ne\) learnability: whether gradient descent actually finds such weights is a different question.
keyPoints: The theorems give no bound on size – the hidden layer may be astronomically large
Depth helps: small deep nets vs. exponentially large shallow nets
Deep ReLU nets of width \(n+1\) are universal approximators on \([0,1]^n\)
Transformers approximate continuous sequence-to-sequence functions
Expressivity ≠ learnability (gradient descent may not find the weights)

name: Describe the setting in which neural networks are related to computability: the type of network, the activation function, the encoding of words into numbers, and the definition of a network recognising a language. What does the definition say about a word that is not in the language?
answer:
Networks considered: recurrent networks (i.e. containing cycles)
• with real weights (in general);
• with one input neuron and one output neuron – the network computes a function \(F:A\to\mathbb R\), where \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\) contains all inputs on which the network stops;
• with the parallel activity rule: output values of all neurons are recomputed in every step;
• with the saturated linear activation function \[ \sigma(\xi)=\begin{cases}1&\xi\ge1,\\ \xi&0\le\xi\le1,\\ 0&\xi\lt0.\end{cases} \] Encoding of words: a word \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{+}\) is encoded into the number \[ \delta(\omega)=\sum_{i=1}^{\lvert\omega\rvert}\frac{\omega(i)}{2^{i}}+\frac{1}{2^{\lvert\omega\rvert+1}}. \] E.g. \(\omega=11001\) gives \(\delta(\omega)=\tfrac12+\tfrac1{2^2}+\tfrac1{2^5}+\tfrac1{2^6}=0.796875\) (\(=0.110011\) in binary). The word is written as binary digits after the point and a final 1 is appended as an end marker, so that words differing e.g. in trailing zeros get different codes.

Recognising a language: a network recognises a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{+}\) if it computes a function \(F:A\to\mathbb R\) (\(A\subseteq\mathbb R\)) such that \[ \omega\in L\iff \delta(\omega)\in A\ \text{ and }\ F(\delta(\omega))\gt0. \] So for \(\omega\in L\) the network must stop on \(\delta(\omega)\) and give a positive output. For \(\omega\notin L\) there are two possibilities: the network does not stop on \(\delta(\omega)\) (so \(\delta(\omega)\notin A\)), or it stops with output \(F(\delta(\omega))\le0\).
keyPoints: Recurrent networks, real weights in general, one input and one output neuron
Parallel activity rule: all neurons recomputed in every step
Activation: 1 for \(\xi\ge1\), \(\xi\) for \(0\le\xi\le1\), 0 for \(\xi\lt0\)
\(\delta(\omega)=\sum\omega(i)/2^i+1/2^{\lvert\omega\rvert+1}\); e.g. \(11001\mapsto0.110011\) (binary)
Recognises \(L\): \(\omega\in L\iff\delta(\omega)\in A\) and \(F(\delta(\omega))\gt0\)
For \(\omega\notin L\): the network does not stop, or stops with \(F\le0\)
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 51–52 (end-marker remark, decimal value and the case of words outside L derived)

name: Which computability results hold for recurrent neural networks with rational and with real weights? (Exact neuron counts need not be memorised, but know the claims and their caveat.)
answer:
Rational weights – Turing equivalence (Siegelmann & Sontag 1995): recurrent networks with rational weights are equivalent to Turing machines.
• For every recursively enumerable language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{+}\) there is a recurrent network with rational weights and less than 1000 neurons which recognises \(L\).
• The halting problem is undecidable already for networks with 25 neurons and rational weights.
• There is a "universal" network (an equivalent of the universal Turing machine).

Real weights – super-Turing power (Siegelmann & Sontag 1994): recurrent networks with real weights are super-Turing powerful.
• For every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{+}\) there is a recurrent network with less than 1000 neurons which recognises \(L\) (including languages that no Turing machine recognises).

Caveat: the computability results need unbounded precision – a whole Turing machine tape is stored in the digits of one neuron's value – whereas real hardware computes with 4–32 bits.
keyPoints: Rational weights: equivalent to Turing machines
Every recursively enumerable language recognised by a small rational-weight network
Halting problem undecidable already for small networks; a universal network exists
Real weights: super-Turing – every language over {0,1} is recognised
Results need unbounded precision (the tape is stored in digits of a neuron's value)

name: Summarise the theoretical results on the expressive power of neural networks, explain why they are "purely theoretical", and compare neural networks with classical computers.
answer:
Neural networks are very strong from the point of view of theory:
• all Boolean functions can be expressed using two-layer networks (one hidden layer);
• two-layer networks may approximate any continuous function (on a bounded closed domain);
• recurrent networks are at least as strong as Turing machines.

These results are purely theoretical:
• "theoretical" networks are extremely huge;
• it is very difficult to handcraft them even for the simplest problems;
• the computability results need unbounded precision (a whole Turing machine tape is stored in the digits of one neuron's value), while real hardware computes with 4–32 bits.
From the practical point of view, the most important advantages of neural networks are learning, generalization and robustness.

Neural networks vs. "classical" computers:
              Neural networks                  "Classical" computers
Data          implicitly in weights            explicitly
Computation   naturally parallel               sequential, localized
Robustness    robust w.r.t. input corruption   changing one bit may completely
              and damage                       crash the computation
Precision     approximate; similar inputs      (typically) precise
              give similar outputs
Programming   learning                         manual
keyPoints: Boolean functions: two-layer networks suffice
Continuous functions on a bounded closed domain: approximated by two-layer networks
Recurrent networks at least as strong as Turing machines
Purely theoretical: huge networks, hard to handcraft, unbounded precision
Practical advantages: learning, generalization, robustness
NN: data in weights, parallel, robust, approximate, learned; classical: explicit, sequential, fragile, precise, programmed
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 53–54 (slide 54 is a table)

name: Outline the history of neural networks in main phases and the scale of today's deep learning: what happened from the first neurocomputers to the current boom, why was there an "AI winter", how large are today's datasets and models, and why are benchmarks called "a treadmill"?
answer:
1. Early neurocomputers (1950s–60s). SNARC (1951, Minsky et al.) was the first hardware neural network; Rosenblatt's Perceptron (1957–60) was the first successful network for image recognition – only one layer of trainable weights, weights realised by potentiometers driven by motors; ADALINE (1960, Widrow & Hoff) was a single-layer network with weights stored in memistors.

2. First AI winter (1969 – early 1980s). Minsky & Papert's Perceptrons (1969) showed the limits of single-layer perceptrons (e.g. XOR) and funding dried up. Key ideas nevertheless appeared: SGD for multilayer networks, reverse-mode automatic differentiation, backpropagation (Werbos 1974), the Neocognitron (1980), Hopfield nets and Kohonen maps (1982).

3. Revival (1986 – late 1990s). Backpropagation was popularised (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams 1986). Dedicated hardware (ASIC, FPGA) was typically not better than software on universal computers.

4. Suppression (late 1990s – ca. 2005) by other ML methods, notably support vector machines.

5. The boom (2006 – now). Deep belief networks (2006) showed that deep networks can be trained; AlexNet won ImageNet in 2012 on two GPUs; transformers (2017) led to large language models; GPUs and specialised hardware (TPU) made the necessary scale affordable.

Scale. Datasets grew to billions of images and about \(10^{13}\) tokens of text for LLMs; model sizes grew to the order of \(10^{12}\) parameters (mixture-of-experts models use only a fraction of the weights per token). In return deep networks have won benchmark after benchmark in vision, speech, language and mathematics.

Benchmark treadmill. Every benchmark starts with low frontier scores, becomes saturated and is replaced by a harder successor; the time from low to high scores has shrunk from years to months. Caveats: mostly self-reported scores, results with vs. without tools differ, data contamination and label errors, and a saturated benchmark no longer says which model is better.
keyPoints: 1951 SNARC, 1957–60 Perceptron, 1960 ADALINE: first hardware networks, one trainable layer
1969 Minsky & Papert show limits of single-layer perceptrons (XOR) → first AI winter
Key ideas (SGD, reverse-mode autodiff, backpropagation) appeared during the winter; 1986 backpropagation popularised
Late 1990s–2005 networks suppressed by SVMs; 2006 deep belief nets, 2012 AlexNet, 2017 transformers
Scale: billions of images, about \(10^{13}\) tokens, about \(10^{12}\) parameters (mixture of experts activates only a fraction)
Benchmark treadmill: saturate and get replaced; caveats: self-reporting, contamination, label errors
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slides 56–60 (history) and 61–68 (scale and benchmarks; condensed, numbers approximate)

name: What matters in AI hardware? Contrast a CPU with a GPU/TPU, list the five hardware parameters with the question each one answers, and say what limits training and what limits inference.
answer:
CPU vs. GPU/TPU: a CPU has a few powerful cores for branching, sequential code; a GPU/TPU has thousands of simple units that multiply matrices – and a layer of a neural network is essentially one matrix multiplication.

Five parameters and their questions:
1. Compute (FLOPS) and number format – how many multiply-adds per second? FP32 \(\to\) BF16 \(\to\) FP8 \(\to\) FP4: every halving of bits roughly doubles throughput.
2. Memory capacity (HBM per GPU) – does the model fit?
3. Memory bandwidth – how fast can the weights be read?
4. Interconnect – how fast do GPUs talk to each other? Scale-up inside a rack (NVLink) vs. much slower scale-out between racks (InfiniBand/Ethernet).
5. Power – today the real limit (kW per rack, GW per cluster).

What limits what: training is mostly limited by compute and interconnect; inference (text generation) by memory – each generated piece needs all weights to be read, so capacity (does it fit?) and bandwidth (how fast can it be read?) decide.
keyPoints: GPU/TPU = thousands of simple units multiplying matrices; a layer ≈ one matrix multiplication
Compute and number format; memory capacity; memory bandwidth; interconnect; power
Halving the bits roughly doubles throughput
Training limited by compute and interconnect
Inference limited by memory capacity and bandwidth

name: Memory wall. Over six years one GPU generation went from compute of \(0.3\) PFLOPS (FP16, 2020) to \(50\) PFLOPS (FP4, 2026) – the course states about \(160\times\) – while HBM bandwidth rose from \(2\) TB/s to \(22\) TB/s (\(11\times\)) and HBM capacity from \(80\) GB to \(288\) GB (\(3.6\times\)). What does this show, why is the gain in compute not mostly "faster cores", and why does it make numerics a first-class topic?
answer:
Memory wall. Compute per GPU grew far faster (\(\approx160\times\)) than memory bandwidth (\(\approx11\times\)) and capacity (\(3.6\times\)). Arithmetic units therefore increasingly wait for data: moving data, not arithmetic, is the bottleneck. This is especially severe for inference, where every generated piece requires reading all the weights once, so the speed is bounded by bandwidth divided by model size.

Where the compute gain comes from: mostly from lower precision (FP16 \(\to\) FP8 \(\to\) FP4; each halving of bits roughly doubles throughput, so \(16\to4\) bits alone gives \(\approx4\times\), derived from the halving rule) and from scale-up – 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain act as one giant GPU – rather than from faster cores. Precision accounts for only about \(4\times\) of the \(\approx160\times\); the remaining \(\approx40\times\) per GPU must come from more and larger specialised matrix units and chip packaging (derived remark; the slide only names lower precision and scale-up), while scale-up mainly raises the compute of the whole system, not of one GPU.

Consequence: since throughput and memory traffic both depend on bits per number, the numerics of training and inference (FP8/FP4 formats) is now a first-class topic in deep learning.
keyPoints: Compute per GPU grew about \(160\times\), bandwidth only about \(11\times\), capacity \(3.6\times\)
Memory wall: moving data, not arithmetic, is the bottleneck
Gains come from lower precision (FP16 → FP8 → FP4) and scale-up, not faster cores
Precision alone explains only about \(4\times\) of the \(160\times\); scale-up raises system, not per-GPU, compute
Fewer bits per number also reduce memory traffic and storage
Numerics (FP8/FP4) is a first-class topic
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slide 74 (table, numbers from the table; 4× precision factor derived)

name: Practical: Use two rules of thumb for AI hardware – "does the model fit into memory?" and "how fast can the weights be read?". Rule given: training needs about 16 bytes per parameter (weights, gradients and the optimizer's bookkeeping) plus memory for forward-pass intermediates; inference needs the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter. A Blackwell GPU has 192 GB, an A100 has 80 GB. For a model with 70 billion parameters, estimate (a) the memory for inference in FP16 (2 bytes) and in FP4 (0.5 byte), (b) the memory for training, and (c) at most how many text pieces per second one GPU with 8 TB/s memory bandwidth can generate for the FP4 model. Explain the reasoning behind each rule.
answer:
Rule 1 – Does it fit? A model with \(P\) parameters needs
• for inference: \(P\times\) (bytes per parameter);
• for training: \(\approx16P\) bytes (weights, gradients and the optimizer's bookkeeping) plus memory for the intermediate results of the forward pass.

(a) Inference, \(P=70\times10^{9}\):
• FP16 = 2 bytes per parameter \(\Rightarrow 70\cdot10^9\cdot2=\mathbf{140\ GB}\), i.e. two A100 GPUs (\(2\cdot 80\) GB);
• FP4 = 0.5 byte per parameter \(\Rightarrow 70\cdot10^9\cdot0.5=\mathbf{35\ GB}\), which fits on one GPU.

(b) Training: \(70\cdot10^{9}\cdot16\) bytes \(=1.12\cdot10^{12}\) bytes \(\approx\mathbf{1.1\ TB}\) for the parameters alone, i.e. at least \(\lceil 1120/192\rceil=6\) Blackwell GPUs – plus the forward-pass intermediates.

Rule 2 – How fast does it write? A language model writes text piece by piece (tokens, roughly word fragments); for every piece, all weights must be read from memory once. Hence \[ \text{pieces/s}\le\frac{\text{memory bandwidth}}{\text{model size in bytes}}. \] (c) \(8\ \text{TB/s}\div35\ \text{GB}\approx\mathbf{230}\) pieces/s at most (\(8000/35\approx229\)).

Consequence: the arithmetic units mostly wait for data. Answering many users at once (each weight is read once and used for all of them) is what makes inference efficient. This is also why inference is limited by memory (capacity and bandwidth) rather than by compute.
keyPoints: Inference memory = parameters × bytes per parameter: 140 GB in FP16, 35 GB in FP4
Training \(\approx16\) bytes per parameter + forward-pass intermediates: \(\approx1.1\) TB, at least 6 GPUs of 192 GB
Each generated piece requires reading all weights once
\(\text{pieces/s}\le\text{bandwidth}/\text{model size}\): at most \(8\ \text{TB/s}\div35\ \text{GB}\approx230\)
Batching many users reuses each weight read – that makes inference efficient
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slide 73 (GPU capacities from slides 71–72, given in the prompt)

name: Give the advantages and disadvantages of doing deep learning in clouds. For each point say briefly why it matters for a student or a company training a large network, and name what kinds of cloud/compute resources exist.
answer:
Kinds of resources. Big commercial clouds (Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure), specialised GPU clouds, and academic infrastructure that is free for students (e.g. MetaCentrum / e-INFRA CZ, IT4Innovations, EuroHPC supercomputers).

Advantages:
• you do not have to care (too much) about technical problems of operating the machines;
• you do not have to buy and optimise high-end hardware, software and networks – important because GPUs, interconnect and cooling are expensive (cf. the hardware parameters);
• scaling on demand and virtually limitless storage – you can rent many GPUs for one large training run.

Disadvantages:
• you do not have full control over the environment;
• performance can vary (shared resources) and there may be connectivity problems;
• you have to pay for the services;
• privacy issues – the data and model leave your own premises.
keyPoints: Resource kinds: commercial clouds, GPU clouds, academic infrastructure
Pro: no operation/technical worries
Pro: no purchase and tuning of expensive hardware
Pro: scaling and virtually limitless storage
Con: no full control, variable performance, connectivity problems
Con: cost and privacy
source: PV021 L2, NN_slides.pdf (2026 deck), slide 75; "why it matters" remarks are interpretation

What both programs do:
• Data: the four XOR inputs \((0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\) with targets \(0,1,1,0\).
• Model: an MLP 2-8-1: a hidden layer of 8 neurons with ReLU and a linear output neuron.
• Initialization: He initialization – weights drawn from a normal distribution with variance \(2/n\), where \(n\) is the number of inputs (fan-in) of the layer, i.e. standard deviation \(\sqrt{2/n}\) – and zero biases.
• Loss: mean squared error \(E=\frac14\sum_{k=1}^{4}(F(x_k)-y_k)^2\).
• Training: 2000 steps of gradient descent on the whole dataset with learning rate \(0.1\): \(w\leftarrow w-0.1\,\partial E/\partial w\).
• Result: the rounded outputs are \(0,1,1,0\), i.e. the network has learned XOR.

PyTorch (object-oriented, eager): parameters are stored inside the layer objects and the optimizer holds references to them. Each iteration calls opt.zero_grad() (clear old gradients), computes the loss, loss.backward() (gradients by automatic differentiation, stored in the parameters) and opt.step() (in-place update).

JAX (functional): parameters are an explicit list of \((W,b)\) pairs passed to pure functions mlp and loss. jax.grad(loss) returns a function that computes the gradients by automatic differentiation; the update is written by hand with jax.tree.map and returns new parameters (nothing is modified in place); @jax.jit compiles the step.

Flax NNX (a third variant from the lecture, not shown in the prompt): the model is a class (nnx.Module) with nnx.Linear layers and the optimizer comes from Optax (optax.sgd(0.1)); the gradient is taken with nnx.grad and the update performed by opt.update.

In all cases the programmer writes only the forward computation and the loss; the gradient comes from automatic differentiation (backpropagation). Frameworks: PyTorch is the de facto standard (eager, define-by-run); JAX is a functional NumPy-like API with composable transformations (grad, jit, vmap) built for TPUs and large-scale training.
